explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "may the name of the God of Jacob protect you." Jacob, the man God renamed Israel, had a God whose name was being trusted to keep somebody safe in a hard day. I think that's a pretty good thing to have in your corner.

I see why you'd go there, friend. Trouble can feel like a test. But the psalm never says that. It says, "may the name of the God of Jacob protect you." The hope in that line is protection, plain and simple.

Hold up, friend. Nothing in this verse is about a judge or a gavel. The psalm says, "may the name of the God of Jacob protect you." It's a line of hope for someone in a rough day, and the hope is protection.

Yes, baker. The psalm says, "May He remember all your gifts and look favorably on your burnt offerings." Those two hopes ride together in the same verse. Then comes a Selah, a pause right there in the song.

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "May He remember all your gifts and look favorably on your burnt offerings." So the burnt offerings are right there in the hope, hiding in the second half. Easy to skate past when the first half is so good.

That's it, baker. The psalm says, "May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed." ALL of them. No plan gets left out in the hallway. That's a big hope to say out loud for somebody.
Ha, I like the sneaky spirit, friend. But the psalm isn't whispering here. It says, "make all your plans succeed." Nothing about hiding them. The hope is that every plan works out.

Peace is a lovely thing to hope for, friend, but it's not what this verse says. The psalm says, "May He give you the desires of your heart and make all your plans succeed." The hope for the plans is success, every last one.

Close, but this one went the other way, friend. The psalm says, "May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God." Shouting and a banner are about as far from quiet as you can get. This victory gets celebrated out loud.

Right, baker. Nobody's keeping this day quiet. The psalm says, "May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God." Shouting AND a banner. I'd be loud too, and I'd probably knock my hat off.
You got it, baker. The psalm says, "May the LORD grant all your petitions." A petition is a request, and the hope is for all of them. That's the last 'may' before the psalm turns a corner.

That sounds nice, friend, but the psalm doesn't say it. The verse ends, "May the LORD grant all your petitions." The hope is about requests being granted, every one of them. Nothing here promises easy.
I can see why that feels right in a psalm like this. But the verse doesn't mention enemies at all. It says, "May the LORD grant all your petitions." The hope is that every request gets granted.

Yes, baker. Look at the shift. After all those 'mays,' the psalm says, "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed." Hoping turns into knowing, and you can hear it in the words. That's a solid place to stand.

I get why you'd guess that, friend, since the song started with a day of trouble. But the turn goes the other way. The psalm says, "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed." That's a voice that knows, not one that shakes.
Patience is a good thing, friend, but it's not the word here. The psalm says, "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed." It moves from hoping to knowing, which is being sure.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "but we trust in the name of the LORD our God." The chariots and horses are on one side, and the name of the LORD is on the other. The song opened with a name too, the name of the God of Jacob.
I see the pull, friend. Chariots and horses sound like army gear. But the psalm says, "we trust in the name of the LORD our God." The trust here isn't in anything an army owns.
Good guess, since earlier the psalm mentions help from the sanctuary. But this line says, "we trust in the name of the LORD our God." The word is name, not a building.
Whoa, hold on, friend. That one flips the verse. The psalm says, "They collapse and fall, but we rise up and stand firm." The ones trusting the LORD's name aren't falling. They're standing.
You nailed it, baker. The psalm says, "They collapse and fall, but we rise up and stand firm." Two groups, two very different endings. The ones trusting the name of the LORD rise up.

That's right, baker. The psalm ends, "O LORD, save the king." The psalm's own opening says it's a psalm of David, so I think a king's name is already in the room. Then the people add, "Answer us on the day we call."

Good thought, since priests and offerings show up earlier, friend. But the last line says, "O LORD, save the king." No high priest is named anywhere in this psalm. The one who gets the cry is the king.
Not this time, friend. The final line says, "O LORD, save the king." A prophet never shows up in the psalm. The one being lifted up in that last cry is the king.
